details: The top grade in A levels. Use the symbol * not the word ‘star’. No apostrophe in the plural.

Explain an abbreviation in full the first time it’s used on a page, then use the initials: Personal Independence Payment (PIP), then PIP. No full stops: BBC, not B.B.C.
No need to explain: BBC, CCTV, DIY, DVLA, EU, GP, HM (in an organisation’s name), HTML, ID, MI5, MI6, MOT, MP, NHS, PAYE, SORN, TV, UK, URL, USA, VAT, VPN; file types (JPG, PDF, PNG); qualifications (BA, GCSE, PhD); letters after names (KC, OBE); abbreviations well known in technical contexts or to the audience.
Only use title case when referring to the name of an academy, like Mossbourne Community Academy. Look at the entry on titles for more on this.
Title case when referring directly to the actual programme, otherwise use lower case.
Title case when referring to the business area covered by Money Laundering Regulations. Do not use the abbreviation.

Title case for Activation, upper case for PIN. Activation PIN has been changed to Activation Code on outgoing correspondence from the Government Gateway. Until all hard-coded instances of Activation PIN have been removed from the Online Services pages, use ‘Activation Code (also known as Activation PIN)’.
Lower case. Only use title case when using the full title: Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004, for example.

Use the active voice rather than the passive voice. This will help us write concise, clear content.
Read the guidance about using clear language for more details on using the active voice.

Put each part of the address on a new line, with the town and postcode on separate lines and no commas at line ends. Put the country, only if users may be writing from abroad, on the line after the postcode.

Address the user as ‘you’ where possible and avoid using gendered pronouns like ‘he’ and ‘she’. Content on the site often makes a direct appeal to citizens and businesses to get involved or take action: ‘You can contact HMRC by phone and email’ or ‘Pay your car tax’, for example.

Title case when referring to the national Adoption Register.
Lower case in subsequent mentions that do not use the full term: the register.
For example, special adviser. Not advisor, but advisory is the correct adjective.

Do not use hyphens in ages unless to avoid confusion, although it’s always best to write in a way that avoids ambiguity. For example, ‘a class of 15 16-year-old students took the A level course’ can be written as ‘15 students aged 16 took the A level course’. Use ‘aged 4 to 16 years’, not ‘4-16 years’.
Avoid using ‘the over 50s’ or ‘under-18s’. Instead, make it clear who’s included: ‘aged 50 years and over’ and ‘aged 17 and under’.
Title case when referring to the Agile Manifesto and principles and processes, otherwise use lower case.
Use allow list as the noun and allow as the verb. Do not use white list or whitelist.

Use UK English spelling and grammar. For example, use ‘organise’ not ‘organize’, ‘modelling’ not ‘modeling’, and ‘fill in a form’, not ‘fill out a form’.
American proper nouns, like 4th Mechanized Brigade or Pearl Harbor, take American English spelling.
Use ‘and’ rather than ‘&’, unless it’s a department’s logo image or a company’s name as it appears on the Companies House register.
Write first as artificial intelligence (AI) then AI throughout.
The abbreviation should come first as it’s more widely known than the full name. Please note that the abbreviation has changed to Bacs.
Use bullet points with a lead-in line, not a table. Use spaces, not hyphens, in sort codes: 60 70 80 (not 60-70-80). No spaces in account numbers unless they are very long (like an IBAN).
Title case if it’s a specific, named team. Always lower case for team and generic names like research team, youth offending team.

Always use billion in money (and million): £138 billion.
Use billions in phrases: billions of people.
Do not use £0.xx billion for amounts less than £1 billion, unless it’s in a sequence where you’re talking about amounts above £1 billion. For example: “There was £15.6 billion spent in August 2024, an increase of £0.2 billion”. If you’re using it outside of the sequence again, use £200 million.
Do not abbreviate billion to b.
Use block list as the noun and block as the verb. Do not use black list or blacklist.
Use 2 words when referring to an article published on a blog. A ‘blog’ is the site on which a blog post is published.
Always lower case unless it’s part of a proper title: so title case for the Judicial Executive Board, but lower case for the DFT’s management board.

Only use bold to indicate interface elements in text that are explicitly telling the user what to do, for example:
1. Select Start.
2. Enter your information then select Done.
Use single quote marks when referring to interface elements in non-instructional contexts, for example: “The ‘Done’ button will always be at the bottom of the page.”
Use bold sparingly - using too much will make it difficult for users to know which parts of your content they need to pay the most attention to.
Do not use bold in other situations, for example to emphasise text.
To emphasise words or phrases, you can:
- front-load sentences
- use headings
- use bullet points
- use callouts

Use (round brackets), but not for something that could be singular or plural: ‘documents’, not ‘document(s)’. Use [square brackets] for explanatory notes in reported speech or for placeholder text: “Thank you [Foreign Minister] Mr Smith.”

You can use the term ‘Brexit’ to provide historical context, but it’s better to use specific dates where possible. For example, use:
- ‘31 January 2020’ rather than ‘Brexit’ or ‘when the UK left the EU’

- ‘after 1 January 2021’ rather than ‘after the transition period’

Reference British nationals by their activity where possible, for example British tourists, British farmers. If you’re talking about them in the general sense, use British people.
Do not use British nationals unless you need to refer to them in a legal context, for example in eligibility criteria. Do not use British citizen unless you’re referring to people with that particular type of British nationality.

Bullets need a lead-in line and more than one bullet, and each should make sense running on from the lead-in. Start bullets in lower case, one sentence per bullet, no ‘or’ or ‘and’ after bullets, no semicolons at the end of bullets and no full stop after the last one.
Numbered steps guide users through a process: they need no lead-in line, and each step is a complete sentence ending in a full stop.

BIC stands for Business Identifier Code (it was previously known as Bank Identifier Code, Bank International Code or Bank Identification Code). Make sure all words are capitalised.

Do not capitalise: government, minister, department, ministry, group, directorate, director general, deputy director or director unless part of a specific name or job title; white paper, green paper, command paper; budget, autumn statement, spring statement unless the full name (2016 Budget); sections or schedules of acts; departmental board, the board; policy themes; select committees in general; the military.
Do not use block capitals for large amounts of text: they are hard to read. Use sentence case.
Lower case in text. Title case in titles: Spencer Tracy, Chairman, GDS.

Lower case in all instances, including ‘the coalition’.

Lower case unless used in the full title, like the National Assembly for Wales (Legislative Competence) (Social Welfare) Order 2008.

Avoid negative contractions like can’t and don’t. Many users find them harder to read, or misread them as the opposite of what they say. Use cannot, instead of can’t.
Avoid complex or conditional contractions such as should’ve, could’ve, would’ve too. These can also be hard to read.

Use lower case when writing about local councils in general. Use capitals for the official name of a local council. For example ‘Reading Borough Council’, ‘Warwick District Council’ and ‘Swanage Town Council’.
When referring to a country or territory, use the names listed in the country register or territory register.

Treat as a singular noun: The data is stored on a secure server.

Months in title case (January), no ordinals (2 June, not 2nd June) and no comma before the year (4 June 2017). Jan, Feb only where space is tight, like tables.
Use ‘to’ in ranges, not hyphens or dashes: tax year 2011 to 2012, 10 November to 21 December.
Use months, not quarters: Jan to Mar 2013, not Q1 2013.
Give the date when saying ‘today’ in news: ‘announced today (14 June 2012)’. For deadlines use ‘on or before’: ‘on or before 6 September 2025’.
Lower case even when referring to the defence team at the MOD.
Lower case except when in the title: the Department of Health and Social Care.
Lower case unless part of a title like Edexcel L2 Diploma in IT.​

Not ‘the disabled’ or ‘people with disabilities’.

One word. Do not use it when talking about an email address. For example, say ‘use this email address’ rather than ‘use this email’.
Write email addresses in full, in lower case and as active links. Do not include any other words in the link text.

Refer to ethnic minority groups individually. Where grouping is necessary, use ‘ethnic minorities’ or ‘people from ethnic minority backgrounds’. Do not use BAME (Black, Asian and minority ethnic) or BME (Black and minority ethnic).
Leave unabbreviated to distinguish from the European Community. Write out in full at first mention, then call it the Commission.

Describe what the user might need to do, rather than what government calls a thing.
Lower case unless the full name of the foundation trust is being used: Salisbury NHS Foundation Trust.
You can make a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, but not a request under the FOI Act.

Make sure text is gender neutral wherever possible, such as ‘them’, ‘their’ or ‘they’.
If you do need to refer to gender, use ‘women’ and ‘men’ rather than ‘males’ and ‘females’. For example, ‘33% of our senior leaders are women’.
Lower case, but title case if referring to a specific election. For example, the 2019 General Election.

Lower case for compass directions and general areas: the north, the south of England, the south-west, north-east Scotland, south Wales, western Europe, the far east, south-east Asia. Title case for names and recognised regions: the South West (administrative region), East End, West End, East Midlands, West Midlands, Middle East, Central America, South America. Write the full name of an area at first use.

Singular noun.

Lower case unless it’s a full title. For example: ‘UK government’, but ‘His Majesty’s Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland’.

Upper case for ‘GOV.UK’. Do not capitalise the first letter in ‘app’.

This is GOV.UK One Login’s main identity proving app. Direct users to this app if they need to prove their identity with GOV.UK One Login.

Always use the definite article. Write ‘the GOV.UK One Login app’, not ‘GOV.UK One Login app’.
Lower case unless part of a school name: The Manchester Grammar School.

Great Britain means England, Scotland and Wales, not Northern Ireland. At first use, write ‘Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales)’ and, where possible, say Northern Ireland is not included; then ‘Great Britain’.
Prefer UK and United Kingdom to Britain and British (UK business, UK foreign policy), but British embassy.
Title case because it’s the name of a programme, but note that it’s Green Deal programme, Green Deal team, Green Deal assessment.

Title case for names of groups, directorates and organisations: Knowledge and Innovation Group.
Lower case when a group has a very generic title like working group or research team.

Lower case unless part of a proper noun: Cardiff Harbour Authority.
One word. You can use head if the context is clear.
Lower case unless it’s the title of an organisation: North East and Central London Health Protection Unit.
Upper case. Do not expand the abbreviation.
Title case for named hurricanes: Hurricane Katrina, Hurricane Sandy.

Do not hyphenate:

Do not use a hyphen unless it’s confusing without it, for example, a little used-car is different from a little-used car. You can also refer to The Guardian style guide for advice on hyphenation.
Use ‘to’ for time ranges and date ranges, not hyphens.
Stands for “Infrastructure as a Service”. Explain the abbreviation at first use.
See the entry on eg, etc and ie.
All names of benefits are title case.
Names of taxes are title case, except input tax.
Do not use italics. Use ‘single quotation marks’ if referring to a document, scheme or initiative.

Specific job titles and ministers’ role titles are title case: Minister for Housing, Home Secretary.
Generic job titles and ministers’ role titles are lower case: director, minister.
See also the entry on Shadow job titles.

Title case, with the apostrophe: Jobseeker’s Allowance. At first use, write ‘New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)’, then ‘New Style JSA’; or ‘income-based Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)’, then ‘income-based JSA’. Use ‘Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)’ and ‘JSA’ only when referring to both benefits.

Title case, with the apostrophe: Jobseeker’s Allowance. At first use, write ‘New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)’, then ‘New Style JSA’; or ‘income-based Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)’, then ‘income-based JSA’. Use ‘Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)’ and ‘JSA’ only when referring to both benefits.

If you have to publish legal jargon, it will be a publication so write a plain English summary.
Where evidence shows there’s a clear user need for including a legal term (like bona vacantia), always explain it in plain English.

Title case if used as the full title: the National Assembly for Wales (Legislative Competence) (Social Welfare) Order 2008.
Lower case otherwise: the legislative competence orders (LCOs) are approved, rejected or withdrawn.

Front-load your link text with the relevant terms and make them active and specific. Always link to online services first. Offer offline alternatives afterwards, when possible.

Use numerals, and spell out measurements at first mention, except kg. No space between the number and an abbreviated unit: 3,500kg, not 3,500 kg. A unit of more than one word (kilometres per hour) is spelled out with its abbreviation at first use, then abbreviated; if used only once, do not abbreviate. Use grams, not grammes. rule: middle-deemed primary school, middle-deemed secondary school

Always use million in money (and billion): £138 million.
Use millions in phrases: millions of people.
Do not use £0.xx million for amounts less than £1 million, unless it’s in a sequence where you’re talking about amounts above £1 million. For example: “There was £15.6 million spent in August 2024, an increase of £0.2 million”. If you’re using it outside of the sequence again, use £200,000.
Do not abbreviate million to m.

Use upper case for the full title, like Minister for Overseas Development.

Use the £ symbol: £75. No decimals unless there are pence: £75.50, not £75.00. Do not write ‘£0.xx million’ or ‘£0.xx billion’, except in a sequence of larger amounts. Write out pence: 4 pence per minute. Currencies are lower case.

After that, use their job title, a title and surname (‘Ms’ for women unless they prefer ‘Mrs’ or ‘Miss’), ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’ and their first name, or their first name in informal content. Avoid titles from other languages, like Herr or Madame.
For the programming language, not “.net” or “.Net”.

Write all numbers as numerals, including 2 to 9, except ‘one’ (use 1 for steps, dates, list points and similar), common expressions (‘one or two of them’), and a number starting a sentence (Thirty-four), unless it’s a date or starts a title or subheading.
Use commas over 999 (9,000), hyphenated words for fractions (two-thirds), numerals for decimals with a 0 before the point (0.5), a % sign (50%), a minus sign (–6), ‘zero degrees’, and ‘500 to 900’, not ‘500-900’ (except in tables). File sizes: 4MB, 569KB, up to 2 decimal places.
Ordinals: first to ninth, then 10th, 11th; numerals in tables; no ordinals in dates (2 June).

If used adjectivally, hyphenate and use one rather than 1.

If an online service has a name that starts with a verb, you do not need to capitalise its name when linking to it. Write the link as part of a sentence so users know what action they can take.

Before the number, add ‘Telephone:’ or ‘Mobile phone:’ – do not use ‘Mobile:’ or ‘Mob:’.
When writing out a number, separate out the area, freephone, mobile or international code from the rest of the number. For example:
- 0131 496 0454
- 020 7946 0457
- 08081 570 422
- 07700 900 265
- +44 (0)29 2018 0542
- +39 1 33 45 70 90
If the number is memorable, group the numbers into easily remembered units. For example, 0800 80 70 60.

Use ‘to’ in time ranges, not hyphens or dashes: 10am to 11am (not 10-11am). Write 5:30pm (not 1730hrs), midnight (not 00:00), midday (not 12 noon, noon or 12pm), 6 hours 30 minutes. Midnight is the start of a day, so consider 11:59pm for a deadline. Add ‘UK time’ if users may be outside the UK.

Page titles should:
- be 65 characters or less
- be unique, clear and descriptive
- be frontloaded and optimised for search
- use a colon to break up longer titles
- not contain dashes or slashes
- not have a full stop at the end
- not be questions
- explain abbreviations unless they are well known - see the entry on abbreviations

Avoid using trademarked names where possible - so tablet not iPad.

Do not refer to the withdrawal agreement to let users know if:

Instead, refer to things which allow a user to understand which group they fall into - for example, if they were living in an EU country before 1 January 2021.

Plain English: avoid these words, unless used in their literal sense as noted.
agenda (unless a meeting): plan. advance: improve. collaborate, liaise: work with. combat (unless military), tackle (unless sport or fishing): solve, stop, deal with. commit, pledge: plan to, we’re going to. counter: prevent. deliver (unless physical things like post or pizzas): make, create, provide. deploy (unless military or software): use, put in place. dialogue: discussion. disincentivise: discourage. empower: allow. facilitate: say how, like ‘run’. focus: work on. foster (unless children): encourage. impact (unless a collision): affect, influence. incentivise: encourage. initiate: start. key (unless it unlocks something): important, or drop it. land (unless aircraft): get, achieve. leverage (unless financial): use, influence. overarching: drop it. progress: work on, develop. promote (unless advertising or careers): recommend, support. robust (unless an object): well thought out. slim down: reduce. streamline: simplify. strengthening (unless structures): be specific. transform: say what changes. utilise: use.
Avoid metaphors: drive: create, cause. drive out: stop, prevent. going forward, moving forward: from now on. in order to: drop it. hub, portal, one-stop shop: website or service (unless part of a name). ring fencing: separate, or ‘money that will be spent on x’.
